docs.title: Module 4: Planning a Data Engineering Product
docs.text:
What problem are we solving and how will we design the solution?

Defining business needs, architecting data solutions, and creating comprehensive blueprints for success.

docs.title: Module 5: Data Engineering Product Development
docs.text:
How do we bring our design to life?

Transforming plans into functional data pipelines, implementing storage solutions, and creating robust processing workflows.

docs.title: Module 6: Data Operations
docs.text:
How do we ensure lasting value?

Deploying, monitoring, and evolving data products to deliver continuous business impact through changing requirements.

docs.title: Knowledge, skills, and behaviours (KSBs)
docs.text: Knowledge, skills, and behaviours (KSBs) are the core attributes which you need to be competent in, to excel in your profession and to pass the end-point assessment (EPA) as part of this apprenticeship.

docs.title: Knowledge
docs.text:
Knowledge refers to the learning you acquire whilst on your apprenticeship. It’s the information covered in the Discover stage and Practise stage activities. Some of the knowledge will be generic, and some will be more specific to your role.

K6: Software development principles for data products, including debugging, version control, and testing.​

K7: Principles of sustainable data products and organisational responsibilities for environmental social governance.​

K9: How to build a data product that complies with regulatory requirements.​

K12: How to cost and build a system whilst ensuring that organisational strategies for sustainable, net zero technologies are considered.​

K13: The implications of financial, strategic and compliance regarding to security, scalability, compliance and cost of local, remote or distributed solutions.​

K21: Policies and strategies to ensure business continuity for operations, particularly in relation to data provision.​

K23: How to undertake analysis and root cause investigation.​

K25: The lifecycle of implementing data solutions in a business, from scoping, though prototyping, development, production, and continuous improvement.​

K30: The methods and techniques used to communicate messages to meet the needs of the audience.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
Skills refer to how you apply the knowledge you have gained in your job. You will develop your skills as you progress through the modules, utilising your on and off-the-job training.

S1: Collate, evaluate and refine user requirements to design the data product.​

S2: Collate, evaluate and refine business requirements including cost, resourcing, and accessibility to design the data product.​

S5: Produce and maintain technical documentation explaining the data product, that meets organisational, technical and non-technical user requirements, retaining critical information.​

S11: Evaluate opportunities to extract value from existing data products through further development, considering costs, environmental impact and potential operational benefits.​

S12: Maintain a working knowledge of data use cases within organisations.​

S14: Identify new tools and technologies and recommend potential opportunities for use in your own department or organisation.​

S22: Develop, maintain collaborative relationships using adaptive business methodology with stakeholders, such as business users, data scientists, data analysts and business intelligence teams.​

S25: Assess and identify gaps in existing tools and technologies in respect of implementing changes required.

docs.title: Behaviours
docs.text:
Behaviours are the way in which you work, and your mindset. You need to act in a way that is appropriate for your organisation and profession.

B1: Acts proactively and takes accountability, adapting positively to changing work priorities, ensuring deadlines are met.​

B2: Works collaboratively with stakeholders and colleagues, developing strong working relationships to achieve common goals. Support an inclusive culture and treat technical and nontechnical colleagues and stakeholders with respect.​

B3: Quality focus that promotes continuous improvement utilising peer review techniques, innovation and creativity to the data system development process to improve processes and address business challenges.​

B4: Takes personal responsibility towards net zero and prioritises environmental sustainability outcomes in how they carry out the duties of their role.​

B5: Use initiative and innovation to problem solve and trouble shoot, providing creative solutions.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Welcome to Module 4: Planning a Data Engineering Product.

Over the next four days, we'll explore the comprehensive process of designing data solutions that deliver real business value.

But before we dive into frameworks and methodologies, I want to start with something you all have experience with.

You've all used digital products. But have you ever stopped to think: How are they designed?

What goes into that process—from idea to something people use every day?

In groups, I want you to imagine you're working for a company that wants to create a new data-driven digital product. Your task is to think through: What steps would you take to design it?

There are no wrong answers here - I want you to draw on your collective experience and knowledge. Think about both the business and technical aspects of design.

  • What information would you need?
  • Who would you involve?
  • What would your process look like?

docs.title: Exercise 1: Brainstorming Design Steps
docs.text:
In groups brainstorm the digital design process, addressing:

  • What are the key phases or stages in designing a data product?
  • What activities happen in each phase?
  • Who needs to be involved at each stage?
  • What inputs and outputs would each stage have?

docs.title: Instructions:
docs.text:
Use your virtual whiteboard to map out the design process as a series of steps.

For each step, note:

  • The name of the phase
  • Key activities involved
  • People/roles who should participate
  • Information needed for this step
  • Outputs produced at this step

docs.title: Deliverable:
docs.text: Be prepared to present your process for 2-3 minutes.

docs.title: Initial Design Process for a Data-Driven Customer Behavior Product
Step 1: Discovery & Requirements Gathering
docs.text:
Activities: - Conduct stakeholder interviews with retail store managers, e-commerce team, inventory managers, and marketing department - Define specific business questions the data product needs to answer - Identify key performance indicators that will measure success - Map existing data sources and assess their quality, completeness, and accessibility - Document regulatory and privacy requirements for customer data

Expected Challenges: - Different stakeholders will have competing priorities between store and online operations - Historical data may be siloed between physical stores and e-commerce platforms - Customer identification across channels may be incomplete (online vs in-store shoppers)

Deliverables: - Business requirements document - Data source inventory - Initial success metrics

docs.title: Step 2: Data Architecture & Integration Planning
docs.text:
Activities: - Design the data integration approach for combining point-of-sale and online transaction data - Create entity relationship diagrams for customer, transaction, and inventory data - Define data quality rules and validation procedures - Establish data refresh frequency requirements (real-time vs. batch) - Design the security model for accessing customer data

Expected Challenges: - Ensuring consistent product identification between store and online systems - Handling varying formats of transaction data from different store systems - Determining appropriate storage solutions for different data types and volumes

Deliverables: - Data integration architecture diagram - Data model documentation - Security and access control plan

docs.title: Step 3: Analytics & Visualization Design
docs.text:
Activities: - Create user personas for different types of business users (store managers, inventory planners, marketers) - Design analytical models for cross-channel customer segmentation - Prototype dashboards for inventory optimization based on cross-channel behavior - Plan personalization algorithms using the integrated customer data - Establish metrics to track the effectiveness of inventory and personalization changes

Expected Challenges: - Designing interfaces that work for users with varying technical expertise - Creating actionable insights that bridge online and offline behavior - Balancing complex analytical capabilities with ease of use

Deliverables: - Dashboard wireframes - Customer segmentation model specifications - Data product user journey maps

docs.title: Key Considerations Specific to This Scenario:
Customer Identity Resolution:
docs.text: A critical early decision is how to match customers across online and in-store purchases to create a unified customer view

docs.title: Data Latency Requirements:
docs.text: We need to determine how quickly inventory decisions need to be made to balance processing costs with business benefits

docs.title: Incremental Delivery Approach
docs.text: I would recommend starting with a specific high-value use case (perhaps optimizing inventory for top 20% of products) rather than trying to solve all problems at once

docs.title: Change Management Strategy
docs.text: Success requires not just technical implementation but also changing how store managers and e-commerce teams make decisions based on the new insights

docs.title: Exercise 2: Apply to a Scenario
docs.text: Apply your phases from the previous exercise to the scenario below.

docs.title: Scenario:
docs.text: A retail company with 200 physical stores and an e-commerce website wants to create a data product that helps them understand customer behavior across both channels to improve inventory management and personalization. They have point-of-sale data, online transaction records, customer profiles, and inventory data available.

docs.title: Task:
docs.text:
Using the design process your group created, outline how you would approach this specific project.

  • What would be your first three phases?
  • List 3 or 4 specific activities for each phase.
  • What challenges do you anticipate?

docs.title: Deliverable:
docs.text: As a group briefly present your design process and initial approach to the scenario. (2-3 minutes)

docs.title: What does the Agile Manifesto say about responding to change?
docs.text:
• Changes are an expected part of the development process and agile teams should have the ability to adapt.
  • Changes to the plan can be made as long as the development team approves the change.
  • Changes can be made once a project manager updates the project plan.
  • The product owner is the only person who can approve plan changes.

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
The Agile Manifesto says that agile teams value responding to change over following a plan. This means that agile teams should expect and value change, even if it is late in the development process. Mature agile teams are prepared for and can adapt to change.

The manifesto does not say anything about how changes are handled, only that there is value in responding to change.

Learn more: https://agilemanifesto.org/

docs.title: Which of the following statements are considered to be part of the Agile Manifesto? (Choose 2 answers)
docs.text:
• Deliver working software frequently, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months, with a preference to the shorter timescale.
  • Changes to requirements late in the development cycle are discouraged to ensure product stability before release.
  • Comprehensive design documentation delivered before development work begins will enhance product quality.
  • The best architectures, requirements, and designs emerge from self-organizing teams

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
The Agile Manifesto is a document often referenced when discussing Agile principles. From this manifesto came 12 guiding principles for teams implementing and practicing agile processes.

Of the choices provided, two answers are among these 12 guiding principles: 1. Deliver working software frequently, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months, with a preference to the shorter timescale. 2. The best architectures, requirements, and designs emerge from self-organizing teams.

The other choices listed are not found among the 12 principles and are counter to the ideas expressed in the Agile Manifesto.

Learn more: http://agilemanifesto.org/principles.html

docs.title: A development team working on maintenance and minor feature requests for an existing application has decided to begin practicing an agile development process.  This team needs to continuously release the product updates as work is completed, and they wish to maximize the flow of their completed work.
docs.text:
Which agile framework is best suited for this team?

  • Kanban
  • Waterfall
  • Extreme programming (XP)
  • Scrum

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
Kanban is a good choice for teams that need to release their product or service as work is completed rather than following a particular cadence associated with practicing scrum. Another advantage of Kanban is that it is beneficial for teams that wish to maximize the flow of work completed.

A waterfall software development process is not considered an agile framework.

Learn more: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban

docs.title: Which of the following statements about Scrum are correct? (Choose 2 answers)
docs.text:
• Scrum should only be used to manage simple projects
  • Scrum is an iterative process framework
  • Scrum defines prescriptive processes for managing project work
  • Scrum is well suited to manage work on complex projects

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
While scrum can be used to manage simple projects, it is particularly well suited to handle complex projects with a non-trivial amount of work to complete. Scrum does not define a prescriptive step-by-step process for managing project work. Instead, scrum is an empirical process where plans evolve based on observations rather than following a theoretical plan. A core concept in scrum is an iteration or sprint. A sprint is a time block that is typically 2 - 4 weeks when a set number of work items are completed.

Learn more: https://app.qa.com/resource/history-of-agile

docs.title: Which of the following statements is in line with an agile mindset?
docs.text:
• The best measure of progress is the number of work items completed by the end of each iteration.
  • The best designs emerge when product owners provide technical guidance in product backlog work items.
  • A team's primary focus should be meeting customer needs, even if it means adapting to changing requirements.
  • When faced with uncertainty, work should not start until product requirements are clearly documented.

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
The statement that is most in line with an agile mindset is:

A team's primary focus should be meeting customer needs, even if it means adapting to changing requirements.

The other statements are not consistent with the Agile Manifesto and not in line with the 12 Principles of agile.

  • The best measure of progress is the number of work items completed by the end of each iteration. --This statement is incorrect because the number of work items is not a perfect measure of progress, particularly if those work items do not meet customer expectations or needs. The best measure of progress is measured by working software that meets customer needs.

  • When faced with uncertainty, work should not start until product requirements are clearly documented. -- This statement is incorrect because even when there is uncertainty, it is best to try something and then solicit feedback from stakeholders and customers. Waiting for complete clarity is counter to agile's idea of iterative development.

  • The best designs emerge when product owners provide technical guidance in product backlog work items. -- This statement is incorrect because the best designs emerge when development teams are given the freedom to self organize and collaborate to find solutions. Technical solutions or information about how a work item should be implemented should not be included in product backlog work items.

Learn more: https://www.agilealliance.org/agile101/12-principles-behind-the-agile-manifesto/

docs.title: Which Agile framework is the most useful in all situations?
docs.text:
• Scrum
  • Kanban
  • DSDM
  • It depends

Not every Agile framework will be right for every team. You need to experiment and do research into different frameworks to make sure you are using the one that is best for you and your team.

Learn more: https://app.qa.com/course/introduction-to-agile-and-scrum-productowner/agile-frameworks/

docs.title: What is currently the number one reason for adopting Agile?
docs.text:
• To accelerate software development
  • To make teams more productive
  • To make teams leaner and able to be reactive to the market
  • To be enable teams to quickly develop a product, regardless of quality

While there are many diverse reasons for adopting Agile, the number one reason right now is to accelerate software development.

Learn more: https://app.qa.com/course/agile-fundamentals-module-1/why-agile/

docs.title: Stacey's process complexity model shows us that Agile thinking is best _______________. (Choose two answers)
docs.text:
• When there is less understanding of the requirements or the solution
  • When there is high certainty
  • When there is high complexity
  • When there is low certainty and low complexity

According to the Stacey’s process complexity model, an Agile approach is best suited for high uncertainty/complexity. A low understanding of requirements or the solution leads to high uncertainty and potentially high complexity.

Adopting an Agile mindset is beneficial for all circumstances.

Learn more: https://app.qa.com/course/agile-fundamentals-module-1/when-agile/

docs.title: Agile is a ______________.
docs.text:
• Mindset
  • Framework
  • Methodology
  • System

Agile is a mindset. While there are many Agile frameworks and methodologies, it really comes down to a way of thinking.

Learn more: https://app.qa.com/course/introduction-to-agile-and-scrum-productowner/what-is-agile/

docs.title: Which Agile principles are the most important?
docs.text:
• Principles 1, 2, 3 & 4
  • Principles 5, 6, 7 & 8
  • Principles 9, 10, 11 & 12
  • All Agile principles are equally important

Every principle is equally important. To work in an Agile way, you need to embrace all 12.

Learn more: https://app.qa.com/course/introduction-to-agile-and-scrum-productowner/principles-of-agile/

docs.title: Which Agile Frameworks focus on the Product Delivery?
docs.text:
• Scrum and PRINCE2
  • Kanban and Scrum
  • AgilePM, DSDM, and PRINCE2
  • AgilePM, DSDM, and Scrum

Frameworks like AgilePM DSDM and PRINCE2 Agile take into account the entire project lifecycle, while Scrum and Kanban focus on product delivery.

Learn more: https://app.qa.com/course/introduction-to-agile-and-scrum-productowner/agile-frameworks/

docs.title: Aside from adopting the Agile principles and values, what else do you need to work in an Agile way?
docs.text:
• Software to track progress
  • Management enthusiasm
  • A Scrum Master
  • None of these answers are correct

Agile is a mindset. You don’t need any of the frameworks to work in an Agile way, if you take on and use the Agile principles and values in your day to day work.

Learn more: https://app.qa.com/course/introduction-to-agile-and-scrum-productowner/principles-of-agile/

docs.title: Which of the following are the essential pillars of the Scrum empirical process? (Choose 3 answers)
docs.text:
• Tools
  • Transparency
  • Inspection
  • Adaptation

If we look at the scrum events, we can see these three pillars at work. For example, the scrum review and daily scrum meetings offer transparency to team members, collaborators, and stakeholders. And, the scrum review and retrospective meetings offer opportunities for both inspection and adaptation.

For more information on these pillars, this Scrum Theory reference provides further information.

Learn more: https://app.qa.com/course/agile-fundamentals-module-2/what-is-scrum/

docs.title: During the daily scrum meeting, a team member raises an issue that is blocking progress of a work item.  What should happen next?
docs.text:
• The team should use the remaining time during the scrum meeting to find a solution for the blocked work item.
  • The team members impacted by the blocked work item should meet after the scrum to discuss solutions.
  • The scrum master will decide whether or not to extend the sprint to complete the work.
  • The work item should be removed from the sprint until a solution is identified, and the developer should take on another task.

If issues or questions arise in the daily scrum meeting that cannot be addressed easily, the team should set aside time outside the scrum meeting to discuss the issue. The scrum master can help facilitate a meeting if needed and help reach out to collaborators or stakeholders. It is not a best practice to change the sprint's length or remove work items from a sprint.

Learn more: https://app.qa.com/course/agile-fundamentals-module-2/scrum-events/

docs.title: Which of the following activities is the Scrum Master's responsibility? (Choose 2 answers)
docs.text:
• guiding the team to help them understand and practice scrum methodologies
  • managing the product backlog by prioritizing work items
  • facilitating scrum events and communication
  • managing the sprint backlog by assigning work to the development team

One of the Scrum Master's primary responsibilities is to be a servant leader that helps and guides the team to understand and practice good scrum methodologies. Part of this servant leadership is to help the team remove obstacles that impede work progress by facilitating communication with collaborators and stakeholders. The Scrum Master also is responsible for facilitating scrum events.

For more information on the scrum master role and responsibilities, look at this Scrum Team reference page.

Learn more: https://app.qa.com/course/agile-fundamentals-module-2/scrum-roles/

docs.title: Which of the following sprint events is used to show / demonstrate sprint results to collaborators and stakeholders?
docs.text:
• The sprint review meeting
  • The daily scrum (stand-up) meeting
  • The sprint planning meeting
  • The sprint retrospective meeting

A sprint review is an event that occurs at the end of a sprint and is a time when the development team presents the product work completed during the sprint to collaborators and stakeholders. During the review, the stakeholders often provide feedback, and this information is incorporated into the product backlog as needed.

For more information on scrum events, take a look at this Scrum Events reference.

Learn more: https://app.qa.com/course/agile-fundamentals-module-2/scrum-events/

docs.title: Which of the following options would be considered good characteristics of a well-defined user story? (Choose 3 answers)
docs.text:
• small
  • negotiable
  • independent
  • prescriptive

You can use the INVEST mnemonic to help remember the key characteristics of a well-written product backlog work item (user story).

A user story should be...

Independent: - The work item should be self-contained and should not be interconnected with other work items.

Negotiable: - The work item should not be overly prescriptive; it should leave room for creative discussion.

Valuable: - The work should provide value to the team, collaborators, or stakeholders.

Estimable: - The work item should contain enough information that the team can estimate its relative work effort.

Small: - The work item should be small enough to fit within a sprint. Ideally, work items should be as small as possible and still provide value.

Testable: The work item should include information in the form of acceptance criteria to be able to test and verify when the work item is complete.

Learn more: https://www.agilealliance.org/glossary/invest/
